facts.statement: The genus Culebrasuchus was named in 2013 by Hastings et al. based on a single skull and three neck vertebrae found in the Culebra Formation.
facts.quote: Culebrasuchus was first described and named by Alexander K. Hastings, Jonathan I. Bloch, Carlos A. Jaramillo, Aldo F. Rincona and Bruce J. Macfadden in 2013 based on a single holotype skull and three neck vertebrae from the Culebra Formation.

facts.statement: Culebrasuchus lived during the Early to Middle Miocene in the Panama Canal Zone.
facts.quote: Culebrasuchus is an extinct, monotypic genus of caiman alligatorid known from the Early to Middle Miocene (Hemingfordian) of the Panama Canal Zone of Panama.

facts.statement: Culebrasuchus was a small animal, similar in size to many living caimans.
facts.quote: Like many living caimans, Culebrasuchus was small in size.

facts.statement: Culebrasuchus possessed upward-opening nostrils and non-overlapping skull bones around the supratemporal fenestrae, traits shared with other caimanines.
facts.quote: Features that Culebrasuchus shares in common with other caimanines include nostrils that open upward (rather than slightly forward, as in alligatorines), and bones that do not overlap the edges of two openings in the skull table called supratemporal fenestrae.

facts.statement: Culebrasuchus had blunt rear teeth and an upper jaw that completely covered the lower jaw when closed, like modern caimanines.
facts.quote: Like living caimanines, Culebrasuchus has blunter teeth at the back of the jaw, and the teeth in the upper jaw completely overly the teeth in the lower jaw when the mouth is closed.

facts.statement: Culebrasuchus lacked ridges above its eye sockets and had a notably large hole in its lower jaw, features not found in other caimanines.
facts.quote: Features in Culebrasuchus that are not found in other caimanines include the lack of ridges above the eye sockets and the large size of a hole in the lower jaw called the external mandibular fenestra.

facts.statement: Culebrasuchus had a straighter lower jaw than most alligatorids, lacked frontal bone ridges between eye sockets, and its largest upper jaw tooth was the fourth instead of the third.
facts.quote: Culebrasuchus also has a straighter lower jaw than most other alligatorids, it lacks the ridges on the frontal bone between the eye sockets that are common among crocodylians, and the fourth tooth of the maxilla (rather than third, as in almost all other alligatorids) is the largest in the upper jaw.

facts.statement: Studies confirm that Culebrasuchus is the most basal member of the subfamily Caimaninae within the family Alligatoridae.
facts.quote: The 2013 study describing and naming Culebrasuchus placed it as the most basal member of the Alligatoridae subfamily Caimanine, and was confirmed by later studies.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the ancestors of Culebrasuchus likely lived in southern Mexico before the species moved into Panama.
facts.quote: The ancestor of Culebrasuchus likely lived farther north, perhaps in what is now southern Mexico, because before the Miocene most of Panama was underwater.

facts.statement: Culebrasuchus was not the earliest caimanine, as other genera like Orthogenysuchus and Eocaiman lived in the Eocene, showing caimanines dispersed across oceans before the Isthmus of Panama formed.
facts.quote: However, Culebrasuchus was not the earliest caimanine; Orthogenysuchus and Tsoabichi are known from the Eocene of North America and Eocaiman is known from the Eocene of South America, indicating that caimanines were dispersing between the continents across large expanses of ocean long before the isthmus formed.

facts.statement: Culebrasuchus lived between 18.5 and 16.3 million years ago during the Burdigalian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Burdigalian to Burdigalian (18.5 to 16.3 million years ago)

rejected.statement: A 2018 study suggested Culebrasuchus might belong to Alligatorinae rather than Caimaninae due to its enigmatic nature.
rejected.quote: Alternatively, a 2018 study by Bona et al. noted that Culebrasuchus was enigmatic and difficult to interpret, and instead proposed it to be a member of Alligatorinae, closely related to the living American Alligator and Chinese Alligator.
